You will gain Prestige for constructing devices, when other players use your devices, and when activating certain components (such as the Patriotic Haiku Generator). The player with the most Prestige at the end of the game is appointed Official Inventor for Her Majesty! Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Action Spaces 2.1 Age I components 2.2 Age II components 2.3 Age III components 3 Game End & Final Scoring 4 2-Player Changes 5 Persona B-side Special Rules 6 Variant Rule Overview Steam Works is a worker placement game in which you are an inventor of ingenious devices, competing for the favour of Her Majesty Queen Victoria. Over the course of the game you will take components from the conveyor belts on the main board, and combine them with power sources to manufacture Devices which function as action spaces for all players. You gain prestige points when an opponent uses a device you manufactured, and from activating certain certain components, and for the components in devices you own. Each player takes one persona board (these can be distributed randomly, or drafted in reverse order of play), and elects to play side A or B. The side A of all boards have different starting resources but the same action spaces available, while side B of each board also has differing action spaces and some special rules. Each turn, you place your leftmost mechanic onto an unoccupied action space (one on your own persona board, or on a power source in any built device). The cost to place a mechanic is printed below that mechanic's space on the persona board; if you cannot (or do not wish to) pay that cost, you may instead pass with that mechanic and collect the same cost instead of paying it. When all players have placed all their mechanics, the round ends. All mechanics return to their owner's persona board, the conveyor belts fill up, and the first player marker advances. If the current age's clock tokens have all been awarded or if there aren't enough tiles left to refill all the open conveyor belts, then the next Age opens: each player gains a mechanic, and a new supply of more powerful tiles becomes available. At the end of Age III the game is over and the player who has the most prestige is declared the winner. Action Spaces The action spaces on side A of the persona board have the following effects: Take the rightmost tile of any conveyor belt. Take a basic power source of your choice. Manufacture a device containing exactly two tiles from your hand. Activate one power source in a device you have already built, without placing a mechanic on it. To manufacture a device you may drag sources and components from your hand and drop them onto the highlighted area of the table. Alternatively, you may click on a tile to select it (giving it a red border), and click again on a destination to move it. You may double-click on a tile to move it from your hand to the manufacturing zone, or from the zone back to your hand. A manufactured device must contain at least one source, and at least one component. A source and a component are connected when the source provides at least one type of power that the component accepts. Invalid connections are allowed to exist in your device but every tile is required to have at least one valid connection. When a mechanic is placed on the power source of a built device, every component connected to it may be activated in the order of the player's choice. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] The very definition of a broken game, because Tasty Minstrel couldn't be bothered to include all of the fucking rules in the fucking rule book! What fucking idiots. I spent nearly two hours trying to figure out this game from the incomplete rules, consulted BGG forums, and finally realized this game is a piece of shit before giving up. Gone from the collection. Too bad, the idea and components look great. I had such high hopes for this one.

[Rating: 2/10] (Played at 4p)  This design felt really forced. The idea of creating machines and using workers to activate them is sound, but I found the massive number of symbols and effects exhausting.

[Rating: 2/10] This has to be one of the worst games we've purchased.  I don't know why, exactly, but it didn't live up to the game we were hoping it would be.  It ended up very confusing to play (and we have several heavier games) and even consulting the rules didn't ease confusion.  It was frustrating and wasn't fun, at all, so we quit halfway through.  This is the first game we have EVER had to give up on halfway through because it was just that bad.

[Rating: 3/10] Sounds so cool but plays so boring. Instead of making awesome massive machines, you make a bunch of small useless ones. The iconography is terrible. Wouldn't recommend. It's a less cool, but more friendly, version of key flower. It's very hard to plan and it's really easy to get screwed. Every round this game goes on it gets less fun.

[Rating: 3/10] --Feb2016-- Likely a very much better game than I'm giving it credit.  But - with four, at least - it's not a game for me.  There's too much information that one needs to have at one's fingertips that's rather hard to track.  And, yet, I expect that one could become better at it with practice, and that it's better (for me, at least) with fewer players.  So I'll likely need to re-rate if I ever have the chance to play with two or three.  And I'm completely disinclined to consider playing with 5!

[Rating: 3/10] The game is too much of the same. Each tile stack is full of duplicate tiles, so machines don't gain much distinction from other machines. Actions become about optimizing tiny differences, which means checking every machine on the table for small differences, which is time consuming and unengaging. Since there is no upgrading available, you just keep building more machines to gain small amount of points, which also makes the play area very busy and hard to interpret. The art is good, and there is nothing specifically wrong with the game, but it's missing engagement and fun.

[Rating: 3/10] Dull and repetitive. So many machines by the end. Didn't really care which one I chose. Just wanted the game to be over.

[Rating: 3/10] Game predominantly involves tile laying, however every single tile needs explaining if you've not played before, often some with complex workings. Game drags on having to investigate / teach what every tile does and adds at least 50% to the playtime. Easy to get bored and frustrated with this.

[Rating: 3.5/10] Not unpleasant; not broken; not problematic. More than anything just not my kind of game.  Quite abstract. Turns go real quick at the start, then they begin to drag as players get more 'machines' in play and there are more options to consider.   Components are nice, though.

[Rating: 3.6/10] Not horrible, but very dull and mediocre game that drags on too long. No one really had fun when we played this. Theme is initially cool, but very quickly evaporates and the game is largely abstract once you are actually playing. The machines are too abstract and generically named to give any sense of what you've "invented" thematically. Playable, but not something I would ever really choose over other games.

[Rating: 4/10] What a waste of an inherently fun mechanism, to tether it to the same old resource to VP conversion and an agonizingly confining decision space. I went from [i]I'm gonna love this game[/i] to being relieved when another player suggested we cut it short by two or three turns.

[Rating: 4/10] A tedious game of combo building and optimization. The iconography is OK, but it becomes difficult to assimilate what the hell everyone has, and how to use it properly. But at the same time, it is difficult to plan since there is a lot of chaos in what gets picked.

[Rating: 4/10] Either we were playing it wrong or the game is extremely boring with two players and should only be a 3++ players game. Feels very unpolished and repetitive to an extent that we played the game only twice before selling. After the first play, we thought we did something wrong. I checked the rules, watched videos and made sure we are not making any mistakes that break the game. Second play was as "strange" as the first one and we started realizing why this game was sold off cheap.
